explanations.explanation: Luke 20:10 says the servant comes to collect the owner's share of the fruit of the vineyard. The tenants work his land, so he wants his cut. Picture a landlord on the first of the month, except he's sending a servant instead of a text. You read that one right, friend.

The half-shekel was an offering to the LORD when Israel was counted (Exodus 30:12-13). That's a whole different thing from this vineyard. Here the servant is sent for the owner's share of the fruit (Luke 20:10). Nobody in this parable is filling out paperwork, friend.

Firstborn males of the livestock belonged to the LORD (Exodus 13:12). That's about animals, though, and this is a vineyard. I don't see one sheep in this story. The servant comes for the owner's share of the fruit (Luke 20:10).

I wish it went that way, friend, but it doesn't. Luke 20:11 says the tenants beat the second servant, treated him shamefully and sent him away empty-handed. So nobody paid anything. The owner's share is still sitting out there uncollected.

That's right. The tenants beat the second servant too, treated him shamefully, and sent him off empty-handed (Luke 20:11). Same trip, same result, just a different servant. If you're keeping score, the owner is zero for two.

explanations.answer: They wound him and throw him out
explanations.explanation: Luke 20:12 says they wounded the third servant and threw him out. No conversation, no cup of tea. It's getting worse with every servant, and I think you can feel it. That's three trips and no fruit.

explanations.answer: They tie him up and keep him
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says they tie him up or keep him. Luke 20:12 says they wounded him and threw him out. He's sent away, not held on to. I think the real answer is hard enough without adding to it.

explanations.answer: They make him work the vines
explanations.explanation: That would be a strange twist, but the text doesn't go there. Luke 20:12 says they wounded the third servant and threw him out. Nobody hands him a pair of pruning shears. These tenants aren't hiring, friend.
Yes, friend. In Luke 20:13 the owner says, “I will send my beloved son.” He has sent three servants and gotten nothing, and now he sends his son. That's the next step in the story.
It's true, actually. After three servants, the owner says, “I will send my beloved son.” (Luke 20:13) He doesn't give up and he doesn't send a fourth servant. He sends his son.

That's the word. The owner says, “Perhaps they will respect him.” (Luke 20:13) The servants came for the fruit and got beaten. Now he's hoping a son will get a different welcome. Hold onto that word, friend.

Paying is what the servants were sent to collect, and they didn't get it. But the owner's hope about his son is different. He says, “Perhaps they will respect him.” (Luke 20:13) The word is respect, friend.
The owner never says anything about following. In Luke 20:13 he says, “Perhaps they will respect him.” He's hoping for respect for his beloved son. Nobody's asking the tenants to join a parade.

That's what they say out loud. The tenants say, “This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Luke 20:14) They talk it over among themselves first. I think that's the coldest part of the whole parable.

The tenants never mention favor. They say, “Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Luke 20:14) After how they treated the three servants, I bet nobody expected a thank-you card. The prize they name is the inheritance.

They don't talk about the harvest at all. In Luke 20:14 they say, “This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” What they're after is the inheritance. That's what they say they'll get.

That's not how Jesus answers it, friend. He says the owner “will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Luke 20:16) So the tenants don't keep it. It's a hard answer, and I think it's meant to be.
That's right. Jesus says the owner “will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Luke 20:16) This is a heavy part of the parable. The vineyard goes to others.

When the people heard it, they said, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) It's the sound of people who didn't like how that sentence ended. They'd followed the story all the way to there. I think it hit them hard.
Nobody's cheering in this crowd. When the people heard it, they said, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) That's a gasp, not applause. It was a very quiet moment, I bet.

The text doesn't say anyone leaves. What it says is that the people respond with, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) And Jesus keeps talking right to them in the next verse. So nobody's heading for the exit yet.

explanations.answer: They will be broken to pieces
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says: “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces.” (Luke 20:18) He's still talking about the stone from Psalm 118:22. I've dropped a few cookies in my time, so I know what broken to pieces looks like, and I wouldn't want to be that stone's landing spot. Serious words, friend.

That's a nicer ending, but it isn't what Jesus says. His words are, “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces.” (Luke 20:18) He's talking about the stone the builders rejected. The result for the one who falls on it is broken pieces.
That's a hopeful guess, friend, but Jesus says something else. He says, “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces.” (Luke 20:18) Strong isn't in that sentence. Broken to pieces is.

Yes. Jesus says, “but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” (Luke 20:18) That's two warnings about the same stone. One is about falling on it, and one is about it falling on you. Neither one is gentle, friend.

It's true, actually. Jesus says, “but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” (Luke 20:18) Right after talking about those who fall on the stone, He says what happens when it falls on someone. Heavy stuff, I know.

That's what Luke 20:19 says: the scribes and chief priests “realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them.” Nobody had to explain it to them. They got it right away. I think that's why things got tense so fast.

explanations.answer: He spoke it against the Romans
explanations.explanation: The Romans don't come up anywhere in this passage. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests realized Jesus had spoken the parable against them. They knew who it pointed at, and it was them.

explanations.answer: He spoke it against the tax collectors
explanations.explanation: Tax collectors don't appear in this passage at all. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests realized He had spoken this parable against them. They didn't need to look around the room to figure it out, friend.

Right. Luke 20:19 says they wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” The people were all around Him there. So the scribes and chief priests held back, even though they wanted to move right then.

The Pharisees aren't mentioned in this passage. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” The crowd listening to the parable is what stopped them.
No soldiers show up in this scene. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests were afraid of the people. The people were right there listening to Jesus, and that held them back.
